subject: Task 21.7 - Provider transport: never follow a redirect (fix SEC-21.5-01) with a non-egress test; independent test-quality audit of tests/ArrTags.Tests/ProviderRedirectTransportTests.cs and the 21.7 transport change
revision: Revised in place after first persistence: TQ-21.7-01's cause was unattributed in the initial version and is now attributed using corroborating evidence from the concurrent docs/implementation/21.7/reviewer-report.json (mtime 14:17), which observed the same working-tree file reverted to the pre-fix shape at 14:15:31 and restored at 14:16:00. summary: The new test class is genuinely discriminating, not decorative, and it establishes the behavior the documentation and the worker report claim. I reproduced all three of the worker's sensitivity probes myself and added a fourth. Probe A (git checkout HEAD of the registrator, i.e. the exact pre-fix registration) -> Failed 5 / Passed 5 / Total 10, deterministic across 3 consecutive runs, with the four ProviderRedirectIsNotFollowedAndTheKeyNeverReachesTheTarget cases failing at line 97 Assert.Empty() on the second loopback origin and the registration-shape case failing at line 130 Assert.NotEmpty(). Probe B (only CreateInsecureHandler left pre-fix) -> Failed 3 / Passed 7, with exactly the two .Insecure redirect cases and the registration case failing on 'ArrTags.Sonarr.Insecure must not follow redirects'. Probe C, which I added (only the ClassifyStatus 3xx arm reverted via the reverse of the two client diffs, handler fix retained) -> Failed 4 / Passed 6, with the four redirect cases failing on Assert.Contains("redirect", ...) because the message fell back to 'The provider returned an unexpected response status.'. So both halves of the fix are independently covered, and the failure mode is the credential-relevant one, not an incidental error. The non-egress assertion is strong: it observes the second origin and asserts it received nothing at all (strictly stronger than 'the key did not reach it'), while the configured origin must have received exactly one request carrying 'X-Api-Key: sec-21-5-01-transport-secret' and no retry (Assert.Single with TransientRetryCount=2). The 'no secret in the error' assertion covers the key value, the body sentinel, the response-header sentinel, and the target origin string, and additionally bounds the message length and pins the code to InvalidResponse/Never. Both positive controls are real, not vacuous: ConfiguredProviderOriginReceivesTheApiKeyHeader asserts the request line, the exact header, and that the key is absent from the request line; TransientServerErrorStillUsesTheConfiguredRetryBound asserts 503 -> ProviderUnavailable/Later with exactly 2 key-bearing requests at TransientRetryCount=1. All four named clients are covered on the real path (ArrHttpClientFactory.CreateClient selects the name from kind + TlsPolicy, and BuildClient asserts connection.TlsPolicy, so allowInsecureTls:true really does exercise the .Insecure name - confirmed by probe B failing only the two .Insecure cases). Guard honesty holds: the class carries no Fact/Theory attribute, no Skip, no JellyfinHostFact, no SkiaNativeTheory, and no PackagedPluginFact, so all 10 cases run in every documented configuration, and the golden-unchanged claim is true (empty git status under tests/ArrTags.Tests/Goldens/, no renderer/RenderVersion/dependency change). Five LOW/INFORMATIONAL findings are recorded and none is a BLOCKER or HIGH: a shared-tree build-output hazard that produced the pre-fix failure signature 4 times in 10 focused runs and that I could not reproduce in 100 subsequent runs; an undocumented load-bearing ordering invariant in the test double on which the non-egress assertion's determinism rests (the 250 ms window is a grace, not the mechanism); documentation drift in docs/release/build-and-release.md, which still carries the 21.3 suite counts and which task 21.8 owns; the 3xx arm being exercised at 302 only; and the insecure-TLS relaxed-certificate path being verified at registration level only, a bound recorded in the worker report but not in the canonical limitations register. PASS_WITH_FINDINGS rather than APPROVED because the documented matrix in docs/release/build-and-release.md no longer matches what the suite establishes (off by 10 passed in all three rows), even though that drift is explicitly assigned to task 21.8 and the deltas themselves are exactly consistent. No test or implementation file was modified; the working tree was restored byte-for-byte (SHA-256 verified) after each probe.

findings.detail: A focused-run burst produced exactly the pre-fix failure signature on a tree whose source was post-fix, and the cause is now attributed with direct evidence from a concurrent agent in the same working tree. Immediately after a clean post-fix build and a passing 10/10 run, a loop of 10 focused `dotnet test --no-build` invocations returned Failed 5 / Passed 5 / Total 10 on runs 4-7 (a contiguous block) and Passed 10/10 on the other six, with the post-fix git diff byte-identical before and after (SHA-256 verified) and nothing of mine mutating the tree. That Failed-5/Passed-5 signature is precisely what probe A (the reverted registration) produces, and the class contains no plausible transient path to failing the four redirect cases plus the pure-DI registration case together. The implementation-reviewer working in parallel at the same time (docs/implementation/21.7/reviewer-report.json, mtime 14:17) independently observed the same event from the other side: after it had restored the registrator and verified sha256 dc9175bf..., a later status check showed the diff at 28 insertions instead of the verified 31, with the insecure handler's `AllowAutoRedirect = false` and comment REMOVED - i.e. exactly the pre-fix defect - at mtime 14:15:31, and the file back to the verified content about 30 seconds later at 14:16:00. That is a revert-probe in this same working tree, and its rebuild is the explanation for my burst. The mechanism is that `dotnet test --no-build` performs no freshness check, so it silently executes whatever ArrTags.dll is in the shared tests/ArrTags.Tests/bin/Release/net10.0 output; the implementation-reviewer makes the complementary point that an incremental build in that window still reported 10/10 because it did not recompile, so a stale or pre-fix binary can produce either a spurious pass or a spurious failure. I could not reproduce the failure in 100 subsequent focused runs (70 immediately after the burst, 30 after my probes were reverted), nor in probe A (3/3 deterministic failures), probe B (1/1), or probe C (1/1), which is consistent with a bounded external window rather than test flakiness. This is an evidence-hygiene risk to the sensitivity record rather than a defect in the test, and it does not invalidate the recorded evidence: I independently reproduced all three of the worker's probes and added a fourth, and the implementation-reviewer independently reproduced probe A as well. It is recorded because a concurrent agent removing and restoring product source in a shared tree is an orchestration-level hazard that both reviews hit, and because a stale binary can make a genuine failure look like a flake or a genuine pass look like a failure.

findings.recommended_action: Not a code change. Three process controls, for any future pre-fix/post-fix evidence run in this repository: (1) force a recompile before reading a `--no-build` result (`dotnet build -t:Rebuild`, since an incremental build can report success from a stale binary); (2) record the identity of the executed binary alongside the result; (3) do not let two agents perform revert-probes or rebuilds in the same working tree concurrently with a recorded evidence run - serialize them, or give each a separate git worktree. The implementation-reviewer's own recommendation, that the reviewed state is only the state at commit time and the task must be re-reviewed if the file is unstable at commit, is the right gate and is consistent with this finding.

findings.detail: The 250 ms RedirectObservationPeriod is sound, but it is a scheduler grace and not the mechanism that makes the non-egress assertion deterministic. The actual guarantee is an undocumented ordering invariant in the RecordingHttpOrigin double: HandleAsync enqueues the recorded request into the ConcurrentQueue *before* it writes the response bytes. Because a followed redirect must complete its second request/response cycle before HttpClient.SendAsync returns, and because the second origin records before it responds, both directions of the assertion are determined before ProbeAsync returns - the positive direction (Assert.Single on the configured origin can never be a race) and the negative direction (a followed hop is always already recorded). That is why the 250 ms delay is neither needed for correctness nor able to mask a followed redirect, and it is why probe A and probe B failed deterministically (4/4 observed runs) rather than flakily. The fragility is that this invariant is load-bearing but not stated at the enqueue/write site, and a future edit that moves the enqueue after the write, or that records only after the client has disconnected, would silently convert Assert.Empty(target.Requests) into a timing-dependent assertion that can pass vacuously while a redirect is still being followed. The class's XML doc and the RedirectObservationPeriod comment describe the grace but not the invariant.

findings.recommended_action: Add a one-line comment at the enqueue site in HandleAsync (and, if useful, a short note in the class doc) stating that recording before responding is what makes the non-egress and single-request assertions deterministic rather than time-bounded. No behaviour change is required; this is a comment-level clarification of a load-bearing invariant.

findings.detail: The new ClassifyStatus arm is a 300-399 range, but the redirect theory only ever serves 302 (RedirectResponse hardcodes PlainResponse(302, "Found", ...)), so 300, 301, 303, 304, 307, and 308 are not individually exercised. The risk is low because the arm is a single C# relational pattern over the status code, not a list, and because 304 Not Modified in particular could not be produced by a redirect-following regression in any case. I also confirmed there is no pre-existing 3xx coverage to lean on: ProviderFailureMatrixTests covers 401/403 (rejected credentials), 409/429/500/502/503 (transient) and 400/422 (invalid request) only, and no test file references HttpStatusCode.Found, MovedPermanently, SeeOther, TemporaryRedirect, PermanentRedirect, MultipleChoices, or NotModified. So this class is the sole coverage of the redirect arm, and it covers one representative code. This is recorded as an observation, not a gap requiring work.

findings.detail: The opt-in insecure-TLS relaxation is verified at two substitute levels and not against a real certificate. AllFourNamedProviderClientsForbidRedirectsAndKeepTheirTlsPolicy asserts, on the real registration, that the two .Insecure names retain HttpClientHandler.ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback and the two strict names do not - a registration-shape check, not a handshake - and the four .Insecure theory cases exercise those clients over plain http:// loopback origins, where certificate validation is never invoked at all. The worker report records this bound honestly in known_limitations and states that it predates the task, so nothing is hidden. The gap I record is one of placement: docs/limitations/accepted.md, whose 'Verification coverage limits' section is the canonical record of what is only partially verified (V1 no live Sonarr/Radarr, V2 unselected cross-runtime runtime, V3 Enhanced coexistence, V4/V5 live-host gaps), contains no entry for the unexercised relaxed-certificate path, and a grep for 'insecure', 'TLS', 'certificate', and 'self-signed' across docs/limitations/*.md returns no match. Since 21.7 now asserts properties of that handler and the new test's class doc and the acceptance criteria speak of the relaxation 'still working for its intended purpose', a reader of the canonical register would not learn that 'works' means 'the callback is present and the redirect setting is off', never 'a self-signed server is accepted'. This bound is not introduced by 21.7, so it is not a 21.7 defect.

substitutes_checked: ArrTagsServiceRegistrator.RegisterServices is invoked for real (BuildServices), so IOptionsMonitor<HttpClientFactoryOptions> and IArrHttpClientFactory come from the production registration, not a hand-built substitute.

SonarrClient and RadarrClient are constructed directly and receive the real IArrHttpClientFactory, so the named-client selection goes through the production ArrHttpClientNames.For(kind, tlsPolicy) path; the redirect theory's four cases therefore exercise all four registered names.

The egress question is not answerable with an in-process HttpMessageHandler double (the pre-existing ProviderFailureMatrixTests shape), because such a double never touches a socket and cannot observe a second origin. ProviderRedirectTransportTests deliberately uses two real loopback TCP origins with a minimal HTTP/1.1 responder, so the credential-egress observation is made at the socket boundary. This is the right substitute choice and the gap it leaves versus the Jellyfin host is recorded in TQ-21.7-05 (no real TLS handshake for the .Insecure names).

ConfigurationSnapshotService, ArrConnectionCatalog, SecretLease, and the two ClassifyStatus methods are all production types on the exercised path; the API key in the recorded request header is the configured value, and no secret is stubbed.

CapturingHandlerBuilder is a test-local HttpMessageHandlerBuilder used only to run the real registered HttpMessageHandlerBuilderActions and capture the configured primary handler. It throws InvalidOperationException on an unrecognized handler type and maps a null primary handler to 'follows redirects = true', so neither an unexpected handler shape nor a bare AddHttpClient registration can pass silently.

Not exercised: no live Jellyfin host, no live Sonarr/Radarr, no self-signed TLS server, and no reverse proxy that legitimately issues 3xx. The first two are pre-existing register entries (V1) and the third is TQ-21.7-05; the fourth is the intended fail-closed behavior documented in ADR-005's implementation note and the changelog.
skips_checked: ProviderRedirectTransportTests.cs contains no [Fact(Skip=...)] , [Theory(Skip=...)], Assert.Skip, or any conditional-skip attribute; grep for 'Skip' and for the four project guard attributes returns no match in the file.

The class is not decorated with JellyfinHostFactAttribute, SkiaNativeTheoryAttribute/SkiaNativeFactAttribute, PackagedPluginFactAttribute, or NonCanonicalRuntimeFactAttribute, so all 10 cases execute in every documented configuration.

Verified by measurement rather than by inspection alone: the default run and the host-guarded run each contribute +10 passed and +0 skipped over their pre-task baselines (1937 vs 1927; 1957 vs 1947), and the forced-native run contributes +10 passed and +0 skipped (2024 vs 2014). The absolute skip counts (66 / 46 / 21) are identical to the pre-task baselines, so no existing skip was widened or newly hidden by this change.
The only staleness in the skip story is the suite-count documentation in docs/release/build-and-release.md, recorded as TQ-21.7-03 and owned by task 21.8.
determinism_checked: No fixed ports: RecordingHttpOrigin binds TcpListener(IPAddress.Loopback, 0) and derives Port from listener.LocalEndpoint, so the two origins per case and the origins across cases cannot collide with each other or with a concurrently running class. The class doc states this intent and the code honours it.

No shared mutable state: the only statics are three const strings and the readonly TimeSpan RedirectObservationPeriod. Each case builds its own ServiceCollection/ServiceProvider (disposed by `using var services`), its own PluginConfiguration, and its own origins. IHttpClientFactory handler-pooling state is per ServiceProvider, so no pooled handler is shared across cases. IOptionsMonitor<HttpClientFactoryOptions> is resolved per case in the registration-shape test.

No order dependence: xUnit runs the cases of a single class sequentially (confirmed by the ~260 ms spacing of the four theory cases in the detailed logger output), and the cases share nothing, so they are order-independent. The class also passed inside the full 2003-test default run.

No wall-clock, network, or process-state dependence: the only timing input is the fixed 250 ms Task.Delay, and all I/O is to 127.0.0.1 loopback origins created in-process. There is no dependence on DateTime.Now, environment variables, or an external process.

The timing race that could matter is a followed redirect arriving after Assert.Empty. It cannot: the origin enqueues the recorded request before writing the response, and SendAsync cannot return before the second response is read, so any followed hop is already recorded when the assertion runs. The 250 ms window is therefore a scheduler grace rather than a race window, and it can neither mask a followed redirect nor cause a spurious failure. Confirmed empirically: 100/100 post-fix passes and 4/4 deterministic pre-fix failures.

Cleanup: both origins are declared with `await using var`, which disposes them in reverse order on both the normal and the assertion-failure path, so a failing test does not leak listeners. RecordingHttpOrigin.DisposeAsync cancels the shutdown token, stops the listener, awaits the accept loop swallowing the expected cancellation/socket/disposal exceptions, and disposes the token source. HandleAsync is fire-and-forget and its own teardown exceptions (IOException, SocketException, ObjectDisposedException) are caught, so an aborted in-flight connection does not surface as an unobserved task exception or as a test-order side effect.

One anomaly I could not attribute or reproduce: see TQ-21.7-01. 4 of 10 focused runs early in this audit produced the exact pre-fix failure signature on a post-fix tree; 100 subsequent runs plus three deterministic pre-fix probes showed no flakiness in the class itself.
limitations: I did not run the live pinned-host matrix (task 21.9's scope) or any Jellyfin-host process, so the fix is verified at the transport/DI level only. Whether a Jellyfin host's global IHttpClientFactory defaults could re-introduce redirect-following is not exercised here; the fix configures an explicit primary handler per name, which is the documented plugin-owned mechanism, but that is reasoned from the registration rather than measured on the host.

All three suite runs were made with the superseded task 21.3 artifacts/ArrTags_1.2.0.0.zip present, so the 3 PackagedPluginFact package-content cases validated that stale archive rather than the corrected build. This conditions the reported counts identically to the worker's and is owned by task 21.8.

The insecure-TLS relaxed-certificate path is not exercised against a real certificate (TQ-21.7-05). The .Insecure clients run over plain HTTP in all 10 cases, so 'the relaxation still works' is established only as 'the dangerous validation callback is present on the .Insecure handlers and absent on the strict handlers, alongside AllowAutoRedirect = false'.

I did not attempt a probe that reverts the registration for one specific *strict* name only (for example ArrTags.Radarr alone). Probe A (all names bare) and probe B (the .Insecure names) bracket that case: probe A shows the loop reaches a per-name failure with the name in the message, and probe B shows the loop discriminates the .Insecure names individually, so the per-name strict case follows by the same construction. The 304/other-3xx statuses were also not individually exercised (TQ-21.7-04).

The anomaly in TQ-21.7-01 is now attributed: the parallel implementation-reviewer (docs/implementation/21.7/reviewer-report.json) was performing its own revert-probe in this same working tree during my failing window, and its rebuild is what my `dotnet test --no-build` runs picked up. The class itself showed no flakiness in 100 consecutive post-fix runs or in any probe. The residual risk is process-level, not test-level: two agents mutating and rebuilding one working tree can make either one's recorded build result unattributable, so the orchestrator should re-verify the registrator sha256 and the full git diff at commit time, as the implementation-reviewer recommends.

This review modified no test, no implementation file, and no canonical document. For the three probes I temporarily replaced src/ArrTags/PluginLifecycle/ArrTagsServiceRegistrator.cs (git checkout HEAD, then two sed deletions) and temporarily reverse-applied the ClassifyStatus diff to the two client files; every file was restored and the restoration was verified by SHA-256 (pre-probe.sha256: all three OK) and by git diff --stat returning the original 9 files / 212 insertions / 7 deletions. The final focused run after restoration was 10/10.

Per docs/agent-contracts.md, this report must be added to task 21.7's reports array in docs/plan/state.json; that entry currently lists only docs/implementation/21.7/worker-report.json, and state.json is outside this reviewer's write scope, so the orchestrator owns the update.
